content: Human bite injuries pose a significant risk to individuals due to the potential for infection by human oral bacteria, which can lead to sepsis. Additionally, there is a risk of transmission of blood-borne diseases, such as syphilis and hepatitis. Injuries caused by involuntary biting, such as those resulting from closed-fist injuries where a fist strikes another person’s teeth, are a common outcome of fistfights. These injuries are particularly concerning when the knuckle joints or tendons of the hand are bitten into, as they tend to be the most severe. Despite their name, love bites are not true bite injuries. They involve bruising caused by suction rather than breaking of the skin. However, actual bite injuries may occasionally occur in the context of fetishistic activities. Proper management of human bite wounds is critical. This includes thorough cleaning of the wound, which involves washing it out, removing any foreign material, and debriding any necrotic or infected tissue. In some cases, surgical consultation may be necessary. Antibiotics play a crucial role in the treatment of human bite injuries, but they are only effective after the wound has been adequately cleaned. The recommended prophylactic antibiotic regimen is amoxicillin/clavulanate 625 mg taken three times daily for at least ten days. For patients who are allergic to penicillin, an alternative regimen includes doxycycline 100 mg twice daily combined with metronidazole 400 mg three times daily. Macrolide antibiotics, such as clarithromycin or erythromycin, should not be used to treat human bite injuries because many human oral commensal bacteria are resistant to these drugs. Similarly, clindamycin is ineffective in this context. Due to the risk of hepatitis B transmission, patients who are not immunized against hepatitis B should be offered a dose of hepatitis B immune globulin, followed by an accelerated course of the hepatitis B vaccine series.
